memories.memory_text: I handed my card to Mrs. Dee like it was something she needed to take, the way you'd press a bill into someone's hand so they wouldn't refuse it — I could feel the ten-dollar bribe still warm in my pocket from the funeral director.
I reached into my pocket for my card, trying to speak to the widow, and the son stepped in front of her, demanding what that was—my card—his voice sharp, confused, then angry.
He slapped the card from my hand, shouted that I didn’t know his father, and told me to get out—then the Finley Huxley grabbed me, pushed me toward the back while the son kept yelling behind me.
I was just trying to talk to someone inside, and the manager told me not to come back, then shoved me—right in front of everyone. I stood there watching people go in, not knowing where to go next.
I threw my law degrees into the wastebasket, one after the other, and stared at the empty wall where they used to hang — it didn't make a bit of difference anymore.
I walked down that dim corridor, file in hand, matching door numbers, feeling the attendants' eyes on me like I didn't belong—then found her room and went in.

I opened the door to the dark ward, unsteady on my feet, and set down my file and the glass badge before pulling out the cheap Polaroid from my bag—I needed pictures of her, proof of what they’d done.
After taking the photos, I sat on the end of her bed, lit a cigarette, and just looked at her—there was no sound, just the tubes and the stillness, and something in me quieted.

I saw her at Northern Care—lying there, unresponsive, the woman Valerie Carter and Dick love like a daughter. I could see the weight of it in Valerie Carter’s voice, how helpless they both felt, and when she asked if I’d seen her, I had to say yes. It wasn’t just a case anymore.

Valerie Carter said this was their chance to get away, her voice breaking—Dick called about the job in Tucson, the Eastwood Press poking around—and I told them, 'I’m going to see you get that chance.' I meant it. Not just the settlement, but their escape. I couldn’t let that slip.

I was juggling these heavy textbooks, trying to get my key out while still reading—couldn't put the book down, not even for a second—because I needed to understand anesthesiology, really understand it, if I was going to make any sense of this case.

I remember the moment Lane Davenport told me Shawn Ellison wanted to meet about testifying—'he wants to testify...?'—and I could feel the case shifting, like the ground finally giving under my feet after all the running in place.

The phone rang, Lane Davenport said it was Graham Keller's office, and when she asked if I wanted to take it, I waved her off—'I'm not in'—but then agreed to a meeting tomorrow at two, knowing full well that call meant they were ready to settle.

Shawn Ellison looked at me and said, 'Her doctors murdered her,' like it was that simple — I remember the weight of those words hitting me, standing there on the stairs, the way he repeated it to make sure I couldn't look away.

I took a cigar from Shawn Ellison, not really thinking, and tried to light it — my hand was shaking, I didn’t even notice I hadn’t bitten the end off, and when I finally got it lit, it felt like I was holding onto something just to keep my hands from showing how much that conversation got to me.

I asked Shawn Ellison why he was doing this, standing there in the cold parking lot, my cigar half-lit, and he just said, 'To do right. Isn't that why you're doing it?' — like he was looking straight through me.

I was on the phone, trying to steady someone who was falling apart, telling them to move on, to go west, that they had their own life — all while my eyes kept drifting to the Polaroids of Sage Hale on the legal pad, and those crossed-out numbers: $250,000, $225,000 circled too many times.

After I hung up, I reached for the bottle and saw her — the blonde in the silver frame, laughing on a sailboat — and next to it, my ring buried in a pile of change, the rosary there too; I just sat in the dark afterward, head back, not moving.
I looked at the settlement number—$210,000—and it hit me how cleanly it divided by three. I’d get seventy thousand. That wasn’t just compensation; it was a cut, a silent share in the cover-up.
I pushed the paper away and said I couldn’t take the money—because if I did, I’d be lost, just a rich ambulance chaser, paid to look the other way like everyone else.

I walked into the lawyers' room, saw Jonah York playing cards, and knew I couldn't wait anymore—I had to get him out of there. I pulled him up and said, 'Come on. Let's get a drink,' then led him into the corridor.
I told Jonah York I turned down the two hundred ten grand because they killed her and are trying to buy it — I can't let that stand. I have to stand up for her, even if he thinks I'm crazy.

I reminded Jonah York of his own words — 'if not now, when' — and asked him to help me, because I can't do this alone. I needed him to see this wasn't just about winning, but about doing something real.

I remember saying that the court isn't there to give the weak justice, but just a chance at it—like that idea kept me going, sitting there with Sawyer Sloane, smoke in the air, the hum of the bar behind us.
I can still feel the pause before I said, 'Maybe I can do something right,' and then her asking if that's what I'd do—like she was testing me—and I told her that's what I was going to try to do.

I walked into the Alex Quincy’s chambers late, saw him eating bacon and eggs with Emery Grayson like they were sharing breakfast at a club, and muttered an apology when he called me out for being late.
When the Alex Quincy tried to push a quick settlement, I cut him off—this wasn’t about deal-making, and I wasn’t there to play along like everything was arranged.
I walked up to the 'Doctors Only' door, opened my the glass badge, and took out the box of Macanudo Cigars—felt the weight of it in my hand—then stepped inside, smiling just a little.

I stood at that door, pounding it like a fool, and when the maid finally answered, she told me Shawn Ellison was unreachable—on some island in the Caribbean with no phone, coming back in a week. I still had the cigars in my hand, useless now, just like me.

I stood at that phone booth in the snow, shivering, trying to get through to Jamie Vale—my fingers numb, the wind cutting through my coat, but I kept pressing the receiver hard against my ear, insisting it was an emergency, that he had to call me back in half an hour.
I told Valerie Carter I’d do my best for her and her sister, and I meant it—more than she could know. It means that much to me.

I stood before the jury, took a breath, and began—telling them how heavy judgment is, how they’ve likely prayed for guidance. I named the two doctors and the hospital, then laid out what we’d prove: Sage Hale was robbed of everything by their negligence.

I told Sweeney I just wanted an even shake — rushed into court in five days, my witness gone, no continuance — but I didn’t back down. I said the hell with it, I’m trying this case and letting the jury decide, even if he’s known as a defendant’s Alex Quincy.

I called him out — told him not to feed me that 'I was a lawyer too' line, that he was a Bag Man then and still is. When he asked if I was done, I said damn right, and told him I’d ask for a mistrial, his disqualification, and have his ass impeached.

I was pressing Graham Mercer on the three-minute gap in the notations after Deborah Kaye's heart stopped, trying to show they weren't doing enough, when he hit me with the anemia explanation—and I realized I’d walked right into it. I’d lost control of the moment, and Jonah York’s look told me everything.
I kept pacing, not stopping, not answering, because I couldn't let it end like this — when Jonah York said the case was over, I turned on him, sharp, like a cornered animal, and made him choose.

dialogue_exemplars: That that poor girl put her trust in the hands of two men who took her life, she's in a coma, her life is gone. She has no family, she has no home, she's tied to a machine, she has no friends -- and the people who should care for her: her Doctors, and you, and me, have been bought off to look the other way. We have been paid to look the other way. I came in here to take your money. (beat) I brought snapshots to show you. So I could get your money.

They might. Yes. That's the point... is that they might... you see, the jury wants to believe. They're all cynics, sure, because they want to believe. I have to go in there tomorrow to find twelve people to hear this case. I'm going to see a hundred people and pick twelve. And every one of them it's written on their face, 'This is a sham. There is no justice...' but in their heart they're saying, 'Maybe... maybe...'
And don't give me this shit, 'I was a lawyer, too.' 'Cause I know who you were. You couldn't hack it as a lawyer. You were Bag Man for the Boys and you still are. I know who you are.
I'm an attorney on trial before the bar. Representing my client. My client, do you understand? You open your mouth and you're losing my case for me.

It's a terrible thing to sit in judgment. So much rides on it. I know that you've thought, 'How can I be pure. How can I be impartial without being cold. How can I be merciful and still be just?' And I know that most of you have said some sort of prayer this morning to be helped. To Alex Quincy correctly. We have the reputation of two men. Two well respected doctors and a renowned hospital before us. And with those two respected men we have my client, Sage Hale...
I'm not through with the witness, your Honor. With all due respect if you are going to try my case for me I would appreciate it if you wouldn't lose it.

Tristan Sterling. Damn right I'm done. I'm going to ask for a mistrial and I'm going to request that you disqualify yourself from sitting on this case. I'm going to take a transcript to the State and ask that they impeach your ass.

I told him my ex-husband was a lawyer, and he didn’t flinch—just said it was wonderful, like he was testing me. I remember how I held back, not saying who ended it, not letting him think he knew me that easy.
He said I came back to see him, and I tried to push back—what if it wasn’t you? But then he just stood up and asked if I’d eaten, like he already knew I’d follow. And I did.
I asked him if they were going to get justice, watching his face in the dim light, the smoke between us curling like doubt.
I leaned in a little, voice low, and asked again—'Is that what you're going to do?'—needing to hear him say it out loud, not just think it.
I said it was all right to leave the picture out, then I started taking off my blouse—my hands were slow, I remember the fabric at my shoulders, and how he just stood there watching.
I asked Jonah York how I was doing, and when he said I was great, I offered him a cigarette and asked what he was drinking—then called the Parker Arden by name, like I belonged there.

I remember sitting at the bar, the weight of Jonah York's story about Tristan Sterling pressing on me—how he started out idealistic, then broken by the system, just like so many others. When Jonah York asked if I liked the story, I just looked at him, unable to speak, the truth of it too heavy to answer.
I asked if he wanted me to leave, and when he said no, I told him to get in bed — that I’d stay with him. Then I led him into the bedroom.
Later, I was sitting in his robe, reading a book, smoking — just watching the bedroom door. I remember putting the book down and taking a slow drag, waiting.
I told him he was talking like a drunk, and when he said it was over, I asked him what he was doing here—if he wanted to leave or even kill himself. I couldn’t let him collapse like that.

He shut himself in the bathroom, couldn’t breathe, and when he screamed at me to stop pressuring him, I opened the door and said, 'You're pressuring yourself.' I had to make him see it wasn’t all on me.
I stepped out into the corridor after the trial, looked around carefully, and walked over to him—just stood there near Tristan Sterling, not saying anything at first.
I asked him if it was over, and then what he was going to do—my voice felt tight, like the words might not come out right, but I needed to know.
He handed me the red-backed document—Confidential, Eyes only—without a smile, just 'Welcome back,' and I took it, feeling the weight of it in my hands.

I picked up the envelope from the floor, opened it by the dim light from the window, and read his handwriting—'I'm going to try. When this is over can we go away?' I just sat there, holding the paper, not moving.

I walked in with the coffee, handed him his, and said I needed to talk—just those words, 'I have to talk to you'—but he didn't stop, didn't really look, just said he couldn't now and went back to the phone, already dialing another number.
I was standing by the wall phone, so tired, when the owner handed me the tray with the coffees and cigarettes—I took the change and turned toward the phone, not sure yet who to call.
I must have fallen asleep on the couch in Northbridge Motel, and when I woke up, I could feel his overcoat over me—he must have put it there.
I was half-awake, cold, wrapped in Tristan Sterling's coat on the couch, and I could feel him standing over me, looking down, before he moved away.

I woke up to the phone ringing, and when Tristan Sterling said he was going to New York, I felt a jolt—like something shifted. I told him I was going too, for the divorce papers, and asked if we could meet at the Beacon, just after four.

After I hung up, Jonah York asked for a cigarette. I didn’t see him go through my purse, didn’t know he’d seen the red-backed report on Tristan Sterling—my notes, the notations. He stood there, quiet, after putting it back. I didn’t know he knew.
I sat there with my coffee, not drinking it, just watching the door—waiting, but not letting myself hope too much.

I saw him walk toward me, and I knew—he finally knew. I tried to say something, but the words wouldn’t come, and then he hit me, knocked me down, the table crashing over. I just kept saying it’s all right, over and over, like that could stop anything.
I stood in the corridor, just watching him—unsure if he saw me, unsure if I wanted him to.
I stood at the end of the corridor holding the yellow paper, my hand trembling, waiting for him to see it—waiting for any sign—but he turned away.

memories.memory_text: I walked in and saw Tristan Sterling passed out on the couch again, bottle on the floor, phone off the hook — same damn mess, same damn man. I told him Valerie Carter called, that he was supposed to be in court, and he didn’t even know who she was.

I knocked the drink out of his hand and slapped him — hard — because he kept treating this like a joke. I told him I was done, that life was too short and I was too old to keep cleaning up after him, then I walked out and slammed the door.
I told Lane Davenport to come back to work — someone had to keep that office running, and she was the only one who wouldn’t screw it up.
I called in a favor with Shawn Ellison’s office and told them to have him reach out — if Tristan Sterling had to drag his ass into this case, at least I’d hand him the witness on a plate.
Tristan Sterling barged in, dragged me up from my gin game, and said he needed to talk—like I wasn't in the middle of a hand. I told my partner not to touch anything before he pulled me out.
I yelled at Tristan Sterling, asking if he was out of his mind for turning down two-hundred-ten grand — what was he going to do, bring the girl back to life?
He kept saying he had to stand up for that girl, and when he reminded me of my own words — 'if not now, when' — I didn't know what to say. He actually made me feel something.

I looked at the notes and told Tristan Sterling the sister's testimony wouldn't work—jury would see right through it, no way to prove the hospital the old radio wrong. But when he pushed Shawn Ellison, I admitted the guy wasn't bad.
I handed Tristan Sterling his cigar box and he asked me to tell Sawyer Sloane he’d meet her later — like I’m his damn messenger now.
